My key takeaways:

• Jurisdiction is half the story. From the US to Paraguay, Ecuador, Guyana, Chile: where the asset sits shapes my gut feel as much as the rock.

• More deal talk than investment talk. Partnerships, JVs, finding the right vehicle, rather than just "buy my stock".

$PENG - BofA hosted CEO Kash Shaikh and management, and came away more convinced.

Buy and $100 price target reiterated, with estimates unchanged. The stock is at ~$49.

Key takeaways from the meeting:

Growth is broadening
It’s no longer just memory. Growth is spreading across AI infrastructure and integrated memory. Penguin has managed 100K+ GPUs and 4.2bn GPU runtime hours, and that operating experience is the edge against OEMs and system integrators.

Services and software are the moat
• Customer contracts of 3–5 years with uptime SLAs
• ClusterWare monitors clusters and fixes issues automatically
• ClusterWare AI adds an agentic layer, priced per GPU
• Works across hardware vendors, so customers aren’t locked into one platform

Inference is a memory story
Bigger models, longer context windows and AI agents all need more memory. Penguin’s CXL-based MemoryAI and KV-cache products move data off scarce HBM, which cuts recomputation and improves token economics. It’s also building a photonics memory appliance with $MRVL to pool memory across racks.

Discipline over growth at any cost
Management is selective with neoclouds, looking at real demand, equity backing, power and financing before signing. The focus is EPS and operating leverage, not maximizing revenue.

- FY27 EPS $4.81 vs $4.57 consensus
- FY28 EPS $5.43
- ~10x FY27 and ~9x FY28 earnings at today’s price

$NVDA We've been thinking about what Nvidia should do with Jensen Huang.

One option we see is for Jensen to become Chairman, with someone else taking over as CEO.

We think losing Jensen completely would be a big loss for Nvidia. His vision, experience, and relationships with customers and partners are incredibly valuable.

text:
In June, Alphabet $GOOGL surprised the market by announcing the mother of all equity raises. The plan was to raise $80 billion, consisting of $15b in convertible preferred stock and $25b in common stock, followed by a $40b ATM set to start in Q3. 

The official reason was to fund AI Capex and pay taxes on employee stock compensation. The timing seemed obvious … they wanted to get ahead of a liquidity crunch as SpaceX $SPCX, OpenAI, and Anthropic lined up their IPOs. SpaceX went public in June, and Anthropic’s November IPO could raise up to $64.4b, with shares expected to start trading on Nasdaq as $ANT on November 19. 

We recently wrote about how the typical IPO underperforms by ~20% on a 3-year horizon. This effect was more pronounced when companies were unprofitable, resulting in an average underperformance of 30%. 

Companies like $SPCX are not set up for patient buy-and-hold investors. Index providers waived the profitability requirement and cut the seasoning window from 90 days to 5. Passive investors will be forced to buy shares just after the initial IPO pump, and just before the accelerated unlock. There’s a 200-year history of finance bros dumping on retail. SpaceX simply figured out how to do it at scale.

- 1-3x fwd P/E memory companies from Samsung to $ESMT. With HBM players now having hyperscaler multi-year price floor LTAs. 

- Optical companies like $POET traded -$97M under net cash. Valuing the operating business very negatively, not even at $0. 

- While AI companies with larger premiums continue to record demand over the next 3-5 years. Such as the new $20B LTAs signed w/ $COHR to $5B LTAs signed w/ $LITE. 

Can someone in the media honestly see negative EV high-beta optical companies, where 2 years of burnrate would still value the company below $0.  

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

Many of these names are extremely profitable today... 

But obviously there's other elements inside the theme, such as: 

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously. 

But everything gets grouped into one with the boogyman of "leverage" or "debt". 

Yes, valuations can compress or correct from macro, potential regulatory uncertainty, or potential capex reductions.

en_summary: @aleabitoreddit finds technical discussion on Sivers helpful but investor messaging too conservative. Cites $NVDA CEO Jensen stating scale-up increases optical volumes by 15x, with $LITE and $COHR quantifying $5-$20B agreements spanning 3-5 years. Criticizes lack of vision for becoming next $40B optical giant, disagrees on portraying company as small given 100m CW DFB capacity coming online and future $GFS volumes, sees tremendous opportunity in CPO/NPO/pluggables.
text:
I found the technical discussion helpful, but investor messaging to be way too conservative.

If you look at how $NVDA CEO describes CPO, Jensen states scale up is increasing optical volumes by 15x. $LITE and $COHR are quantifying that by describing $5-$20B agreements spanning 3-5 years out.

Having this question, and not talking about Ayar, O-Net, Poet, or ELS partnerships. Then redirecting the question to near term pluggables seems off.

The vision also needs work, “communications and sensing” semi company is very unexciting.

It’s technically true, but there’s no vision being communicated on being the next $40B optical giant or what Sivers is going to be in the next 5 years that would attract long term holders.

The core valuation Sivers gets is from optical opportunities, I also personally disagree that it’s helpful to loop back to former cellular relationships when talking about future $GFS volumes

I disagree when you portray the company as “small” when Sivers 100m CW DFB capacity is coming online, alongside large foundry partners.

Which is a material % of the world’s annual laser capacity.

Investors want to hear about future economic opportunities and how you fill the gap with more qualifications during a bottleneck.

Sivers has a tremendous opportunity for CPO/NPO/Pluggables but I’m afraid it’s not being communicated properly. 

It’s understandable here since EETimes is more technical oriented, but I hope this messaging gets communicated better in the next earnings
